title: The Morning Jason Njoku Switched Off iROKOtv's Free Service
dek: In April 2014 the founder of Nigeria's biggest Nollywood streaming site gave up millions in advertising to make viewers pay.

story.event: Ending iROKOtv's free, advertising-funded service and moving to subscription only
story.summary: iROKOtv began in 2010 as a free, advertising-funded YouTube channel of licensed Nollywood films and grew into a freemium streaming site. On 28 April 2014 Jason Njoku announced he would kill the free service, moving viewers in 140 countries to subscription only because a free viewer earned about $0.15 a month against about $6 for a paying one. Within days he closed the London office, and by July the whole service was subscription-only.
paragraphs: Early on 28 April 2014, Jason Njoku published a blog post titled "Killing iROKOtv." Four years before, after what he called five and a half years of failing at everything he tried, he had started a YouTube channel, NollywoodLove, to put Nigerian films online legally. The idea came at his family home in Manchester, where his mother loved Nollywood films that were hard to find. He went to Nigeria and won over wary producers. In 2011, he later wrote, YouTube advertising was all of the company's revenue.

By 2014 iROKOtv was a freemium site built over about two and a half years: 95 per cent of viewers watched free with adverts and 5 per cent paid. Advertising had brought in several million dollars the year before. But in 140 countries, Njoku wrote, a free viewer was worth about $0.15 a month and a paying one about $6. Free Nollywood films from producers who would not sell to iROKO were piling up on YouTube, and rivals backed by mobile operators were arriving. A fortnight earlier he had told AFP, "we are not profitable, we have a long way to go."

He chose to switch the free service off. From that morning, viewers in those 140 countries, more than 400,000 unique visitors a month, would be moved to a paid-only service with a 14-day free trial and no adverts; the rest of the world would follow. "I am literally betting the entire company and millions of dollars of revenue on a dramatic shift to a paid only model," he wrote. He named the danger as well: speed and results would decide whether iROKO became a case study or "a cautionary tale of over ambition and hubris." Investors had just added $4 million to an $8 million round, and about 90 people worked for him.

Within days he closed the London office, where 12 people worked. "This wasn't easy," he wrote. By late July the whole service was subscription-only, and he said he expected to lose "something like 95 per cent" of its traffic before the year was out. In January 2016 iROKO announced $19 million in content and capital deals with the French media group Canal+ and an existing investor, Kinnevik. By 2017 it relied mostly on subscriptions.

quote.text: people in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success. If they were careful at the end, as (they should be) at the beginning, they would not so ruin them.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi warns that affairs are most often ruined on the eve of success. Njoku feared the same thing and called it hubris. Whether ending a free service that brought in millions was the careful act or the careless one, the story leaves open.

reflection: Many of us run a free tier without calling it that: the unpaid favour that became a habit, the extra shift nobody counts, the project kept alive because it once mattered. Njoku's numbers made his choice visible, fifteen cents against six dollars. Yours will rarely be so tidy, but they can still be counted in hours, energy and what each thing gives back.
Laozi adds a caution. A change made in a rush of fighting talk can undo what was nearly working. Some decisions are better weighed on a rested morning than at the end of a draining day.
invitation: Pick one thing you keep doing for free out of habit. Write down what it costs you each week and what it gives back, and look at the two side by side.

cross_checks.claim: On 28 April 2014 Njoku announced on his blog that iROKOtv would kill its free, ad-supported service and move to subscription only.
A free viewer earned about $0.15 a month against about $6 for a paying viewer.
Njoku wrote that he was betting the entire company on a shift to a paid-only model.
iROKO began in 2010 as a YouTube channel of Nollywood films before launching its own platform in 2011.
YouTube's share of iROKO's revenue had fallen sharply after the paid service launched.

research_notes: Episode changed from the slate's 2011 move off YouTube to the better-documented April 2014 decision to end the free service, which completes that move; the 2010-2012 shift from YouTube is told as background. YouTube share: Njoku's blog says YouTube went from 100% of revenue in 2011 to about 12% by April 2014; Techzim (2013) reports 14.1% in the first half of 2013; the figures cover different periods and the story uses only the 2011 starting point. Audience figures differ: the blog says the 140 countries had over 400,000 monthly uniques; ITWeb reports 1 million monthly unique visitors from 178 countries overall; AFP says nearly a million hits a month; Business Daily cites more than 500,000 registered users. The story uses the blog's 140-country figure. Price: the blog says paid users were on $5 (three-month commitments); AFP and Business Daily give $7.99 a month for the subscription; the story gives no price. The free service was not ended everywhere at once: the blog starts with 140 countries, and by late July Business Daily describes the whole service as subscription-only. 'Within days' for the London closure: ITWeb reported it on 30 April 2014, two days after the subscription post. The blog is cited from a Wayback Machine capture because jason.com.ng no longer resolves. WIPO's account of the idea's origin at his mother's home is the magazine's summary, not a direct Njoku quotation. Later results (subscriber numbers, profitability) were not found in reliable sources and are not claimed; the story ends with the 2016 funding and WIPO's 2017 note that the business relied mostly on subscriptions. Funding is venture (the blog's $8M December 2013 round plus $4M; AFP notes a US-based investment fund). Wikipedia was not used.
